title: A Gate-Based Quantum Computing Framework for Codon Optimization
authors: Fatemeh Ghasemi, Kion Kim
abstract: Codon optimization is a challenging combinatorial optimization problem with important applications in synthetic biology, protein expression, and biotechnology. While quantum annealing has previously been explored for this problem, the application of gate-based quantum algorithms remains largely unexplored. In this work, we present a gate-based quantum computing framework for codon optimization by formulating the optimization objective as an Ising Hamiltonian and expressing it in terms of Pauli operators suitable for gate-based quantum processors. The proposed framework is investigated using the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE), Sampling Variational Quantum Eigensolver (SVQE), and the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), with benchmarking against exact diagonalization, classical optimization, and quantum annealing. Using a three-amino-acid benchmark, the proposed implementations successfully reproduce the exact ground-state solutions while identifying optimized ansatz selections, optimization strategies, initialization schemes, and hardware execution settings that provide reproducible performance on current noisy quantum hardware. Hardware demonstrations are performed on IBM Quantum processors to evaluate the practical implementation of the proposed workflow. As a work in progress, this study establishes a reproducible computational framework for gate-based quantum codon optimization and provides the foundation for future investigations of larger protein sequences as quantum hardware and algorithms continue to advance.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that codon optimization can be reformulated as an Ising Hamiltonian and solved with gate-based quantum algorithms such as VQE, SVQE, and QAOA.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a reproducible quantum workflow for a biologically relevant combinatorial optimization problem, with potential impact on protein engineering and synthetic biology.
method: Encode codon optimization as an Ising model with Pauli operators.
Solve the objective using VQE, SVQE, and QAOA.
Benchmark against exact diagonalization, classical optimization, and quantum annealing, then test on IBM Quantum hardware.
infographic.evidence_signal: On a three-amino-acid benchmark, the methods reproduced the exact ground-state solutions and were evaluated for ansatz choice, initialization, optimization strategy, and hardware settings.
infographic.watch_item: Results are currently limited to a small benchmark, so scaling to larger protein sequences may face noise, circuit depth, and hardware connectivity constraints.
infographic.paper_title: A Gate-Based Quantum Computing Framework for Codon Optimization

title: TATVA: A Reinforcement Learning Framework for Quantum Circuit Synthesis
authors: Om Bhamare, Aryan Jadhav, Manas Shinde, Prithvi Shinde
abstract: One of the most important initial steps in quantum computing is high-fidelity quantum state preparation, because errors in it can affect the final computational result. Therefore, one of the major challenges is to design a quantum circuit that can achieve the desired target state accurately with a smaller number of gates. Traditionally, circuits are designed using predefined rules and mathematical decompositions, but this makes it difficult to design circuits for different and complex target states. This paper presents TATVA, a reinforcement learning (RL) system for synthesizing quantum circuits. TATVA views circuit synthesis as a sequential decision problem in which the agents select one gate at a time and calculate the fidelity after each applied gate, with the gate producing the highest fidelity selected for the circuit. The system introduces a parallel architecture that uses two RL agents, Deep Q-Network (DQN) and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), along with Qiskit's statevector simulator. The system can synthesize up to 5 qubits while achieving a fidelity of 0.999999 and producing compact circuits. After achieving the desired fidelity, it performs a post-hoc optimization step that reduces the circuit depth while preserving the achieved fidelity. The circuit is finalized using fidelity, success rate, gate count, and circuit depth. Target states that are not used during training are used to test whether the system has learned effectively and can generalize beyond the training states. This approach aims to enable automatic quantum circuit synthesis with high fidelity using reinforcement learning.

infographic.key_insight: TATVA frames quantum circuit synthesis as a sequential reinforcement-learning problem, using DQN and PPO to build compact high-fidelity circuits gate by gate.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It offers an automated path to prepare quantum states with fewer hand-designed rules, which is useful for scalable quantum algorithm compilation and near-term hardware workflows.
method: Two RL agents (DQN and PPO) propose gates one step at a time.
After each gate, fidelity is evaluated and the best action is selected.
A post-hoc optimization step reduces circuit depth while preserving fidelity.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports synthesis up to 5 qubits, achieving fidelity as high as 0.999999 and testing generalization on target states not seen during training.
infographic.watch_item: Results may depend on simulator fidelity and the approach could be harder to scale as qubit count and action space grow.
infographic.paper_title: TATVA: A Reinforcement Learning Framework for Quantum Circuit Synthesis

title: Hardware-Efficient Ground-State Preparation using Variational Imaginary-Time Majorana Evolution
authors: Federico Santona, Manuel G. Algaba, Aeishah Ameera Anuar, Anna M. Wernbacher, Prachi Sharma, Fedor Šimkovic
abstract: Compact ground-state preparation circuits are essential for early fault-tolerant quantum chemistry. We introduce Variational Imaginary-time Majorana Evolution (VIME), a classical pre-training algorithm that extends operator-projected variational quantum imaginary-time evolution (OVQITE) to molecular electronic structure using a single compiled Majorana-propagation (MP) surrogate graph. We pair VIME with a compressed tiled Unitary Product State (c-tUPS) ansatz that we develop to reduce both classical simulation and quantum state-preparation costs. In the strongly correlated ruthenium complex TLD-1411, active-space calculations requiring up to 52 qubits achieve chemical precision against DMRG reference energies, with energy errors approximately $400\times$ smaller than those from ADAPT-VQE-based variational Majorana-propagation (ADAPT-VMPE). Across the strongly multireference acene series up to heptacene (60 qubits), VIME matches or improves on the MP-reported energy accuracy of the ADAPT-VMPE comparison points with up to $26\times$ fewer CNOTs and $167\times$ lower two-qubit depth. These results establish imaginary-time classical pre-training of compressed variational ansätze as a promising route to resource-efficient molecular ground-state preparation.

infographic.key_insight: VIME uses classical imaginary-time pre-training plus a compressed ansatz to prepare molecular ground states with much lower quantum resource cost than prior variational Majorana methods.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach targets near-term fault-tolerant quantum chemistry by cutting CNOT count and two-qubit depth while preserving chemically accurate energies on challenging correlated molecules.
method: Extends OVQITE to molecular electronic structure via a single compiled Majorana-propagation surrogate graph
Pairs the algorithm with a compressed tiled Unitary Product State (c-tUPS) ansatz to reduce simulation and state-preparation cost
Uses classical pre-training before quantum execution to improve hardware efficiency
infographic.evidence_signal: On TLD-1411 and acene benchmarks up to 60 qubits, VIME reaches chemical precision and matches or improves ADAPT-VMPE accuracy with up to 26× fewer CNOTs and 167× lower two-qubit depth.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on the quality of the surrogate graph, ansatz compression, and active-space setup, so benefits may vary across molecules and hardware constraints.
infographic.paper_title: Hardware-Efficient Ground-State Preparation using Variational Imaginary-Time Majorana Evolution

title: Fourier Symmetrization for Geometric Quantum Machine Learning
authors: Letao Wang, Abdel Lisser, Sreejith Sreekumar, Zeno Toffano
abstract: Geometric quantum machine learning incorporates symmetry into quantum models, but how symmetry shapes their expressivity and guides effective model design remains insufficiently understood. We address this question through the Fourier representation of quantum Fourier models (QFMs). Symmetry organizes the frequency spectrum into orbits and sums the Fourier coefficients within each orbit into a symmetrized coefficient. When QFM trainable layers form independent exact 2-designs, the variance of each symmetrized coefficient equals the sum of the coefficient variances in its orbit. For single-layer QFMs with $\varepsilon$-approximate 2-design trainable layers, we bound the deviation from this identity. The resulting bound for individual Fourier coefficients can be exponentially tighter than an existing bound. The hyperoctahedral group provides an example of orbit growth that can mitigate vanishing expressivity of the symmetrized coefficients. Symmetrization of QFMs over an elementary abelian 2-group also yields pure multivariate Chebyshev polynomial basis functions. We introduce randomized encoding, which implements invariant models without ancilla qubits or the additional circuit depth for quantum twirling. We evaluate the models as quantum physics-informed neural networks (QPINNs) on two-dimensional screened Poisson and stationary viscous Hamilton-Jacobi equations. Under hard boundary constraints, QPINNs using exact symmetrization and randomized encoding achieve the lowest mean errors in the two benchmarks, respectively.

infographic.key_insight: Symmetry in quantum Fourier models reorganizes Fourier frequencies into orbits, enabling exact variance relations and stronger control of expressivity under symmetrization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The paper provides practical symmetry-aware design rules and a randomized encoding method that can implement invariant quantum models without ancillas or extra twirling depth.
method: Group Fourier coefficients into symmetry orbits and define symmetrized coefficients by summing within each orbit.
Derive variance identities for exact 2-design trainable layers and deviation bounds for single-layer \u03b5-approximate 2-designs.
Use randomized encoding to realize invariant QFMs efficiently, and test them as QPINNs on PDE benchmarks.
infographic.evidence_signal: In two-dimensional screened Poisson and stationary viscous Hamilton-Jacobi benchmarks, hard-boundary QPINNs with exact symmetrization and randomized encoding achieved the lowest mean errors in their respective tests.
infographic.watch_item: The strongest theoretical guarantees rely on exact or near-2-design assumptions, so practical performance may depend on how well real trainable layers approximate these regimes.
infographic.paper_title: Fourier Symmetrization for Geometric Quantum Machine Learning

title: On the pseudorandomness of simple quantum processes
authors: Jesko Dujmovic, Jonas Haferkamp, Alexander Poremba
abstract: Can simple processes appear highly complex? Gowers (Comb. Prob. Comp. '96) conjectured that repeatedly composing local random reversible operations can yield global permutations that are indistinguishable from random. In this work, we study the unitary quantum analog of this question, in an attempt to make new progress on this longstanding conjecture. Our first result shows that statistical moment matching in the form of unitary designs does not generically lead to pseudorandomness---even for the simplest quantum processes: for every fixed $t$, we give an efficiently samplable family $\{ν_n\}_n$ of distributions on one- and two-qubit gates such that, after $T=O_t(n^2\log^2 n)$ independent steps, the resulting $n$-qubit ensemble is an approximate unitary $t$-design with negligible error $\exp(-Ω(\log^2 n))$, yet an efficient quantum algorithm distinguishes it from random using only $O_t(\log^2 n)$ queries. This refutes the unitary analog of the Hoory--Magen--Myers--Rackoff conjecture (ICALP '04) for permutations. Our second result is a stronger separation between unitary designs and pseudorandom unitaries at polynomially bounded moments; our counterexample, however, requires highly structured ensembles, in contrast with the simple local walks from before. This suggests caution when using unitary designs to model information scrambling in black-hole physics, as even maximally scrambled systems can exhibit structure which is accessible to efficient experiments. Motivated by these findings, we then propose new conjectures for how pseudorandomness can plausibly emerge within simple quantum processes, such as random quantum circuits.

infographic.key_insight: Simple local quantum processes can look highly scrambled in moments (as unitary designs) yet still be efficiently distinguishable from truly random unitaries, so design-like behavior does not imply pseudorandomness.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For quantum circuit design, verification, and black-hole-inspired simulation, this means moment-matching metrics alone are insufficient to certify randomness or information scrambling.
method: Construct efficiently samplable distributions over 1- and 2-qubit gates.
Analyze the resulting n-qubit ensemble after O_t(n^2 log^2 n) independent steps.
Compare unitary-design properties against distinguishability by an efficient quantum query algorithm.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports approximate unitary t-designs with negligible error exp(-Ω(log^2 n)) but still an efficient distinguisher using only O_t(log^2 n) queries.
infographic.watch_item: The strongest separation beyond local walks uses highly structured ensembles, so the counterexample may not directly generalize to natural random-circuit implementations.
infographic.paper_title: On the pseudorandomness of simple quantum processes

title: Quantum Circuit Pruning: From NISQ Architectures to Fault-Tolerant Operations
authors: Pau Escofet, Carmen G. Almudéver, Sergi Abadal, Eduard Alarcón
abstract: We present a routing-aware pruning strategy for quantum circuits that selectively removes parametric two-qubit gates whose computational contribution is outweighed by the fidelity cost of their execution, and assess it across both Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) and fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) architectures. Each two-qubit gate of a circuit is evaluated by comparing an architecture-independent lower bound on the fidelity cost of omitting the gate against a hardware-specific model for the routing execution cost in each setting. We additionally provide an analytical characterization of the pruning boundary as a function of rotation angle, qubit distance, and hardware noise. Simulations on benchmark circuits demonstrate gate count reductions of up to 48.6% and fidelity improvements of up to 47.7% in the NISQ regime, while a feasibility analysis on FT hardware indicates that pruning is expected to remain relevant across a range of code distances and physical error rates. These results establish routing-aware pruning as a practical and unified compilation strategy across the quantum computing stack.

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces routing-aware pruning that removes two-qubit parametric gates when their expected fidelity benefit is lower than the cost of executing them on a given quantum architecture.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a unified compilation rule for both NISQ and fault-tolerant systems, helping reduce circuit depth, gate count, and routing overhead while improving end-to-end fidelity.
method: Compare an architecture-independent lower bound for omitting a gate against hardware-specific execution cost.
Evaluate each two-qubit gate based on rotation angle, qubit distance, and noise level.
Use the pruning boundary to decide whether a gate should be kept or removed across NISQ and FTQC settings.
infographic.evidence_signal: Benchmarks show up to 48.6% fewer gates and up to 47.7% fidelity improvement in NISQ simulations, with FTQC analysis indicating pruning remains useful across multiple code distances and physical error rates.
infographic.watch_item: Pruning decisions depend on accurate hardware cost and noise models, so performance may degrade if calibration or routing estimates are inaccurate.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Circuit Pruning: From NISQ Architectures to Fault-Tolerant Operations

title: Two-Stage Quantum-Classical Distribution Network Reconfiguration via Cycle-Edge Encoding
authors: Nowar Alashkar, Cade Kennedy, Phillip C. Lotshaw, Shaked Regev, Miguel Angel Lopez-Ruiz, Ananth Kaushik
abstract: Distribution network reconfiguration (DNR) is a combinatorial optimization problem that seeks a low-loss network topology subject to topological and electrical operating constraints. In this work, we propose a two-stage quantum-classical method for DNR. First, an iterative linear-ramp Quantum Alternating Operator Ansatz (LR-QAOA) searches topologically feasible subspaces constructed using a novel cycle-edge encoding. The encoding guarantees that every represented configuration is a spanning tree while allowing the size and coverage of each subspace to be adjusted to the available qubit budget. Second, the resulting sample distribution is used to guide a mixed-integer second-order-cone programming (MISOCP) solver. The method is evaluated on six distribution networks ranging from 33 to 417 buses through simulation and execution on trapped-ion quantum hardware. Across all six test systems, the MISOCP solver guided by hardware-derived distributions reaches an incumbent within 1\% of the best-known solution in less median solver time than the corresponding unguided solver.

infographic.key_insight: A two-stage quantum-classical pipeline uses LR-QAOA with cycle-edge encoding to generate feasible distribution-network topologies, then steers a MISOCP solver toward lower-loss reconfiguration solutions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This approach offers a hardware-aware way to accelerate distribution network reconfiguration while respecting spanning-tree feasibility and electrical constraints.
method: Cycle-edge encoding restricts the quantum search space to spanning-tree configurations.
Iterative LR-QAOA samples feasible topologies within a qubit-budgeted subspace.
Hardware-derived samples guide a downstream MISOCP solver to refine the best topology.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across six benchmark networks (33 to 417 buses), hardware-guided MISOCP reached an incumbent within 1% of the best-known solution in less median solver time than an unguided solver.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on how well the sampled quantum distribution transfers to the classical optimizer, and the approach may be limited by qubit budget and hardware noise.
infographic.paper_title: Two-Stage Quantum-Classical Distribution Network Reconfiguration via Cycle-Edge Encoding

title: Adaptivity is all you need: Optimal stabilizer learning using just single-copy measurements
authors: L. Bittel, J. Eisert, W. Gong, A. A. Mele, L. Schatzki
abstract: Stabilizer states are central to quantum computing, underlying quantum error correction, benchmarking, and efficient classical simulation. Yet their learnability exhibits a striking gap: an $n$-qubit stabilizer state can be learned from $Θ(n)$ copies using two-copy Bell measurements, whereas non-adaptive single-copy measurements require $Ω(n^2)$ copies. Here we show that adaptivity completely closes this gap. We give a polynomial-time adaptive algorithm that learns an arbitrary $n$-qubit stabilizer state from $Θ(n)$ single-copy Clifford measurements, matching the optimal sample complexity of Bell sampling without any multi-copy measurements. The same ideas yield a sample-optimal single-copy tolerant tester and, with $k$ qubits of quantum memory, the optimal testing tradeoff $Θ(n-k+1/\varepsilon)$ at infidelity $\varepsilon$. Finally, we show that this adaptive mechanism extends beyond exact stabilizer states: states of stabilizer nullity at most $r$, including states prepared by Clifford circuits with a bounded number of $T$ gates, can be learned using $O(n2^{r})$ single-copy measurements.

infographic.key_insight: Adaptive single-copy Clifford measurements can learn any n-qubit stabilizer state with optimal Θ(n) sample complexity, closing the gap to two-copy Bell-measurement methods.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This reduces measurement overhead for quantum state characterization, improving practical workflows for error-correction benchmarking, verification, and stabilizer-based simulation.
method: Use adaptive, polynomial-time single-copy Clifford measurements instead of multi-copy Bell measurements.
Exploit measurement choices conditioned on previous outcomes to recover the stabilizer structure efficiently.
Extend the same adaptive strategy to tolerant testing and low-nullity near-stabilizer states.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports optimal Θ(n) learning with single-copy measurements, a sample-optimal tolerant tester, a Θ(n-k+1/ε) testing tradeoff with k qubits of memory, and O(n2^r) scaling for states of stabilizer nullity at most r.
infographic.watch_item: The approach relies on adaptive measurement control and Clifford-capable hardware, so runtime and coherence constraints may limit performance in near-term implementations.
infographic.paper_title: Adaptivity is all you need: Optimal stabilizer learning using just single-copy measurements

title: QPI-DeepONet-MAC: A Scalable and Stable Hybrid Classical-Quantum Architecture for Physics-Informed Deep Operator Networks
authors: Said Lantigua, José Valencia, Gilson Giraldi, Renato Portugal, Jonas Maziero
abstract: General operator learning for parametric partial differential equations (PDEs) is a fundamental challenge at the intersection of artificial intelligence and physics-based modeling. Physics-informed Deep Operator Networks (PI-DeepONets) incorporate governing equations into learning, but face optimization difficulties in high dimensions. Quantum extensions offer additional representational capacity, yet their trainability can be hindered by barren plateaus. Here, we introduce QPI-DeepONet-MAC, a hybrid quantum-classical architecture that integrates parameterized quantum circuits into PI-DeepONets through a multiplicative-and-additive coupling (MAC) of classical representations and quantum expectation values. We prove analytically that the proposed architecture retains universal operator approximation capabilities. Furthermore, we derive bounds on quantum parameter gradients, establishing explicit conditions to avoid barren plateaus alongside a scaling criterion for trainability. Additionally, we derive a lower bound on the number of sensors required for a target accuracy, directly linking sampling requirements to input function regularity, domain dimension, and PDE dynamical growth. Finally, we propose an informational regularization scheme based on quantum coherence and state fidelity dynamics to prevent coherence loss and preserve quantum structure during training. Together, these results establish a theoretical foundation for quantum-enhanced physics-informed operator learning and position QPI-DeepONet-MAC as a scalable, stable framework for solving parametric PDEs.

infographic.key_insight: QPI-DeepONet-MAC is a hybrid classical-quantum physics-informed operator network that aims to keep DeepONet expressivity while improving trainability and stability for solving parametric PDEs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could enable scalable surrogate models for high-dimensional physics simulations, especially where classical PI-DeepONets struggle with optimization and sample efficiency.
method: Uses a multiplicative-and-additive coupling (MAC) between classical DeepONet features and quantum expectation values.
Integrates parameterized quantum circuits into a physics-informed operator-learning pipeline.
Adds analytical trainability and regularization tools to reduce barren plateaus and coherence loss.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports analytic proofs and derived bounds: universal operator approximation, gradient bounds for avoiding barren plateaus, and a lower bound on required sensors tied to regularity, dimension, and PDE growth.
infographic.watch_item: Practical performance may depend on circuit size, noise sensitivity, and whether the quantum components remain trainable at scale on near-term hardware.
infographic.paper_title: QPI-DeepONet-MAC: A Scalable and Stable Hybrid Classical-Quantum Architecture for Physics-Informed Deep Operator Networks

title: Neural Fourier Surrogates for Data Reuploading Quantum Neural Networks
authors: Oliver Knitter, Jonathan Mei, Sang Hyub Kim, Chi Chen, Masako Yamada, Martin Roetteler
abstract: For quantum machine learning, the exact boundary between classical and quantum advantage is still poorly understood. Direct comparison between quantum neural networks (QNNs) and existing classical models, which encompass fundamentally different function classes, often fails to provide broader insight into the difference between the two. Inspired by the techniques of Neural Quantum States and Random Fourier Features, this work introduces Neural Fourier Surrogates (NFS), a stochastic classical neural network architecture for efficiently learning coefficients over the same finite Fourier series support as quantum neural networks. Testing on a selection of tabular benchmark datasets, we find that NFS is an effective classifier architecture broadly competitive with established classical baselines, including a comparable Random Fourier Features model, and possessing comparable performance to data-reuploading QNNs; combined with additional analysis comparing the learned Fourier spectra of QNNs and NFS on synthetic data, these results establish NFS as a natural classical baseline for evaluating QNN performance.

infographic.key_insight: Neural Fourier Surrogates (NFS) provide a classical stochastic baseline that learns the same finite Fourier support as data-reuploading QNNs, enabling a more direct comparison of quantum and classical expressivity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For quantum ML practitioners, NFS offers a practical benchmark to test whether QNN gains come from quantum effects or from Fourier-spectrum capacity that can be matched classically.
method: Uses a stochastic neural architecture to estimate coefficients over a finite Fourier series support.
Draws inspiration from Neural Quantum States and Random Fourier Features.
Compares learned Fourier spectra of QNNs and NFS on synthetic data.
infographic.evidence_signal: On tabular benchmark datasets, NFS is reported to be broadly competitive with standard classical baselines and comparable to data-reuploading QNNs.
infographic.watch_item: Because NFS is a surrogate baseline rather than a quantum model, parity in performance does not by itself demonstrate quantum advantage or absence of hardware-related constraints.
infographic.paper_title: Neural Fourier Surrogates for Data Reuploading Quantum Neural Networks

title: Trapdoored Clifford Operators and Applications
authors: Minki Hhan, Hojune Lee
abstract: Random Clifford operators have numerous applications in quantum computing, including randomized benchmarking, classical shadows, and quantum authentication. However, sampling and implementing uniformly random $n$-qubit Clifford incur near-quadratic complexity due to the size of Clifford group. We introduce a cryptographic way to overcome these barriers: trapdoored Clifford operator distributions whose samples are computationally indistinguishable from uniformly random Cliffords, yet implementing them can be much faster given the trapdoor. We construct a distribution of trapdoored Clifford operators whose elements can be sampled and implemented in near-linear time under a variant of the learning parity with noise assumption. Our constructions allow fast tableau action on Pauli labels for classical simulation, and also can be optimized to admit polylogarithmic-depth implementation. Along the way, we construct trapdoored matrices over finite fields that support efficient multiplication by both a matrix and its inverse, resolving an open question left by Vaikuntanathan and Zamir [SODA'26]. We use these constructions to obtain faster protocols based on random Cliffords. We also explore their applications to the worst-case to average-case reductions for matrix and Clifford problems including the iterated matrix multiplication and Clifford circuit synthesis. In particular, we show the hardness of batching Clifford circuits: synthesizing circuits that apply the same Clifford to multiple registers is at least as hard as worst-case matrix multiplication, even when synthesis succeeds on a small constant fraction of random Cliffords. This extends to approximate implementations by general quantum circuits.

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces trapdoored Clifford distributions that look random to outsiders but can be sampled and implemented much faster when a secret trapdoor is available.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This could make randomized benchmarking, classical shadows, quantum authentication, and related Clifford-based protocols far more practical for larger quantum systems.
method: Constructs trapdoored Clifford operators under a learning-parity-with-noise-style assumption.
Provides fast tableau updates for classical simulation and polylog-depth implementation options.
Builds trapdoored finite-field matrices with efficient forward and inverse multiplication, enabling Clifford and matrix applications.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports cryptographic indistinguishability guarantees, near-linear sampling/implementation, polylog-depth variants, and hardness reductions tied to matrix multiplication and Clifford synthesis.
infographic.watch_item: The speedups and security properties depend on cryptographic assumptions, so practical deployment may be limited if those assumptions weaken or if trapdoor generation becomes costly.
infographic.paper_title: Trapdoored Clifford Operators and Applications

title: Toward Optimal Circuit Depth for Geometrically Local Hamiltonian Simulation
authors: Zhenyu Shen, Yusen Wu, Penghui Yao, Xiao Yuan, Yukun Zhang
abstract: Understanding the dynamics of interacting quantum systems is a central goal of quantum simulation. For geometrically local Hamiltonians, locality suggests that digital simulation should retain much of the parallelism of the underlying dynamics. For a target accuracy $ε$, we construct a nearest-neighbor quantum circuit that simulates the dynamics of an $n$-qubit, time-independent, finite-range Hamiltonian with normalized local interaction strength on a fixed-dimensional lattice for time $T\ge1$, with circuit depth $O(T\log(nT/ε))$ and gate count $O(nT\log(nT/ε))$. This reduces the polylogarithmic overhead of Haah, Hastings, Kothari, and Low to a single logarithm. On logarithmic-scale blocks from the Lieb--Robinson decomposition, a shallow but highly accurate implementation is essential for reducing the circuit depth. Our key observation is that spatial localization also controls the cost of high precision. In each block, the error of a constant-order product formula is compensated for by a correction, yielding exponential accuracy. The correction can be implemented with depth proportional to the block diameter, introducing no additional asymptotic depth scale beyond that required by spatial localization. Furthermore, we prove an unconditional circuit-depth lower bound for uniform XXZ Hamiltonians: at fixed evolution time $T$ in the stated regime and sufficiently small fixed error $ε$, any nearest-neighbor quantum circuit simulating these dynamics requires depth $Ω(\log n/\log\log n)$. This matches our $O(\log n)$ upper bound up to a doubly logarithmic factor, establishing near-optimal circuit depth for lattice Hamiltonian simulation in this regime. Together, these results clarify the role of locality and precision in determining the circuit complexity of quantum dynamics and suggest broader principles for spatially constrained quantum computation.

infographic.key_insight: Geometric locality lets Hamiltonian simulation be done in nearly optimal nearest-neighbor depth: the paper reduces the overhead to O(T log(nT/ε)) and proves a matching lower bound up to a doubly logarithmic factor for XXZ dynamics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For quantum hardware with local connectivity, this suggests time evolution can be compiled with shallow circuits whose depth scales mainly with lattice size, evolution time, and target precision rather than with full-system complexity.
method: Use a Lieb–Robinson-style spatial block decomposition to organize the simulation into logarithmic-scale regions.
Within each block, combine a constant-order product formula with a correction step to recover exponential accuracy.
Implement the correction with depth proportional to block diameter, avoiding extra asymptotic depth overhead.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports an upper bound of O(T log(nT/ε)) circuit depth and O(nT log(nT/ε)) gate count, plus an unconditional lower bound of Ω(log n/log log n) for uniform XXZ Hamiltonians at fixed T and small ε.
infographic.watch_item: The result is asymptotic and relies on finite-range, geometrically local Hamiltonians on a fixed-dimensional lattice, so constant factors and hardware-specific compilation overhead may still matter in practice.
infographic.paper_title: Toward Optimal Circuit Depth for Geometrically Local Hamiltonian Simulation

title: First-quantized quantum simulation with non-local potentials by matrix-product-state encoding
authors: Kazuki Tsuoka, Taichi Kosugi, Masari Watanabe, Hirofumi Nishi, Yu-ichiro Matsushita
abstract: Quantum simulations based on first-quantized approaches can offer lower space and gate complexities than second-quantized approaches. The gate requirements for these simulations can be further reduced by employing pseudopotentials, a technique widely used in classical quantum chemistry calculations to decrease the number of simulated electrons. However, implementing pseudopotentials in quantum circuits remains challenging due to their non-local nature. In this study, we proposed a method to efficiently implement non-local potentials using matrix product state (MPS) encoding. MPS encoding allows us to efficiently implement a Trotter step operator with a circuit depth of $O(\mathrm{deg}(V_{\mathrm{loc}}) n^{\mathrm{deg}(V_{\mathrm{loc}})} + 8Lnn_{\mathrm{atom}}χ^2 + 2n^2)$, where $\mathrm{deg}(V_{\mathrm{loc}})$ is the degree of the polynomial local potential, $n_{\mathrm{atom}}$ is the number of atoms in the system, $L$ is the maximum number of projector functions across all atoms, and $n$ is the number of qubits used to represent the binary-encoded wave function in one-dimensional space. We demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to a model of the ionization of a one-dimensional hydrogen atom driven by an ultrashort laser pulse. Our results showed that MPS encoding significantly reduces the required circuit depth compared to a direct unitary decomposition, providing a pathway for practical first-quantized simulations.

infographic.key_insight: Matrix-product-state (MPS) encoding makes non-local pseudopotentials practical in first-quantized quantum simulation by sharply lowering Trotter-step circuit depth.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a more hardware-feasible route to quantum chemistry and strong-field simulation, especially where pseudopotentials reduce electron count but introduce difficult non-local operators.
method: Encode the wave function in MPS form instead of direct unitary decomposition
Implement non-local pseudopotentials efficiently through the MPS structure
Combine with first-quantized Trotterization to reduce depth to O(deg(V_loc) n^deg(V_loc) + 8Lnn_atomχ^2 + 2n^2)
infographic.evidence_signal: The authors tested the approach on ionization of a one-dimensional hydrogen atom driven by an ultrashort laser pulse and reported significantly lower circuit depth than direct unitary decomposition.
infographic.watch_item: The depth advantage depends on MPS bond dimension χ and pseudopotential structure, so performance may degrade for more entangled or higher-dimensional systems.
infographic.paper_title: First-quantized quantum simulation with non-local potentials by matrix-product-state encoding

title: Exponential quantum advantages for decoded quantum interferometry in the streaming setting
authors: Kewen Wu, Guangxu Yang
abstract: Decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) is a polynomial-time quantum algorithm introduced by Jordan et al. (Nature 2025). For a natural optimization problem, known as optimal polynomial intersection (OPI), it achieves approximation guarantees in regimes where all known classical algorithms require exponential time. Besides time, space is another central resource: storing and manipulating a massive input can be very challenging, especially when logical qubits carry substantial fault-tolerant implementation overhead. This motivates the following question: does DQI yield quantum advantages in memory, and can we prove it unconditionally? We give an affirmative answer to this question in the streaming setting. In particular, we consider a natural generalization of OPI using Hermite interpolation and Hasse derivatives, which asks for a low-degree polynomial satisfying as many constraints on its values and derivatives as possible. As a concrete example, we show [Quantum efficiency.] An adaptation of the DQI algorithm produces a polynomial satisfying $93\%$ of the constraints; moreover, it only reads the input stream in one pass, uses polylogarithmic space, and has polylogarithmic computation time per stream entry. [Classical hardness.] Any classical algorithm that produces an answer satisfying just $76\%$ of the constraints requires polynomial space, even if it can read the input stream with polynomially many passes and can use unlimited time. Our result provides a complete tradeoff curve for the tunable parameters, and implies that DQI has provable quantum advantages for the original OPI problem.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that decoded quantum interferometry can give an unconditional streaming-memory advantage, with a quantum algorithm solving a Hermite-interpolation generalization of optimal polynomial intersection using polylogarithmic space where classical methods need polynomial space.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This matters for memory-constrained quantum and classical data processing because it demonstrates a concrete setting where quantum algorithms reduce storage and per-item processing cost, not just runtime.
method: Adapt DQI to a streaming version of Hermite interpolation with values and Hasse-derivative constraints.
Use a one-pass quantum algorithm with polylogarithmic space and polylogarithmic time per streamed entry.
Prove a classical lower bound even for multi-pass algorithms with unlimited time.
infographic.evidence_signal: From the abstract, the quantum method satisfies 93% of constraints, while any classical algorithm achieving only 76% satisfaction still requires polynomial space.
infographic.watch_item: The advantage is established for a specific generalized streaming formulation and approximation threshold, so practical gains may depend on how well real hardware can support the required quantum memory and fault tolerance.
infographic.paper_title: Exponential quantum advantages for decoded quantum interferometry in the streaming setting

title: Zero- Versus Infinite-Temperature Damping in Variational Quantum Circuits: Feature Scale, Sampling Cost, and Frame Gauge
authors: Vu-Quoc-Minh Nguyen, Tuan-Vu Truong, Hoang-Long Nguyen, Trung-Khanh Le
abstract: The Pauli twirl of amplitude damping (AD) is generalized amplitude damping at infinite temperature: it keeps the contraction of AD and removes its non-unital term, so comparing the two in variational circuits isolates the zero-temperature bias, which acts mainly through the scale of the features. For random parameters, features under AD settle on a floor, which at strong damping is set by the last layer, has a closed form, and at fixed $T_1$ falls with temperature as $\tanh(\hbarω/2k_BT)$; under the twirls they shrink by a constant factor per layer, up to eight qubits. A trainable output scale removes most of the resulting accuracy differences, leaving AD ahead of its twirls by at most about three percentage points in our simulations; what it removes reappears as a cost in measurement shots: trained and tested with $10^3$ shots per image, a four-qubit classifier under AD at $p=0.3$ stays within 1.5 points of noiseless accuracy, while the twirled classifiers lose up to 33. At weaker damping the separation depth grows roughly as $(np)^{-1}\ln(1/p)$. The damping direction is a gauge when the damping follows complete entangling layers and the circuit boundaries are trainable; in an eigensolver it becomes physical inside a decomposed two-qubit gate.

infographic.key_insight: Amplitude damping mainly changes variational quantum circuit features by a zero-temperature bias, while its infinite-temperature twirl preserves contraction but removes that bias, so accuracy differences are often a feature-scaling effect rather than pure noise strength.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A trainable output scale can recover much of the lost accuracy, but the price shifts to higher measurement-shot cost, making noise-model choice and calibration important for practical quantum ML hardware deployment.
method: Compare amplitude damping with its Pauli-twirled infinite-temperature counterpart in variational circuits
Analyze feature scaling, sampling cost, and depth dependence under random parameters and trained models
Study when damping direction is gauge-dependent versus physically meaningful in circuit layouts
infographic.evidence_signal: Across simulations up to eight qubits, AD and its twirls differ by only about 3 percentage points after output scaling, while a four-qubit classifier at p=0.3 and 10^3 shots/image stays within 1.5 points of noiseless accuracy under AD but loses up to 33 points under the twirled models.
infographic.watch_item: The damping direction can be a gauge only in certain circuit architectures; in decomposed two-qubit gates or eigensolver settings, it becomes a physical effect and cannot be ignored.
infographic.paper_title: Zero- Versus Infinite-Temperature Damping in Variational Quantum Circuits: Feature Scale, Sampling Cost, and Frame Gauge

title: Beyond Feasibility: Finite-Depth Accessibility in Constrained QAOA
authors: Rushikesh Ubale, Gregory T. Byrd, Yasar Mulani, Sangram Deshpande
abstract: Constraint-preserving mixers keep QAOA within a feasible subspace, but feasibility and global mixer connectivity do not determine which feasible configurations are available to a particular shallow circuit. We study constrained QAOA at the level of the circuit actually executed: a specified feasible initial state, finite depth, and finite schedule of mixer interactions. We define the finite-depth accessible set $R_p(M,x_0)$ and show that the computational-basis support of the ideal QAOA circuit is contained within it. This gives a parameter-independent objective ceiling $f_R^\star=\max_{x\in R_p}f(x)$ and a normalized reachable-quality diagnostic $Q_R$, separating accessible volume from the objective quality contained within it. We evaluate this framework using resource-matched block-local XY mixer schedules for constrained portfolio optimization and synthetic block-constrained quadratic problems. Across 207 favorable-tail CVaR QAOA configurations, $Q_R$ shows the strongest association with realized shallow-QAOA performance among the structural diagnostics considered, with Pearson and Spearman correlations of $0.7003$ and $0.8057$; the relationship remains positive under controlled and dependence-aware analyses. The distinction persists across changes in feasible initialization, portfolio size, and objective family. A compilation-only study further shows that, for the dense portfolio Hamiltonians considered here, phase-separator routing dominates the compiled two-qubit resource scale, while mixer schedules with comparable compiled two-qubit cost can exhibit markedly different finite-depth accessible quality. These results motivate objective-relevant finite-depth accessibility as a complementary diagnostic for resource-bounded constrained QAOA.

infographic.key_insight: Feasibility alone is not enough: for constrained QAOA, the shallow circuit can only reach a finite-depth accessible set, and the quality of that reachable set predicts performance better than global mixer connectivity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a practical, parameter-independent way to judge whether a constrained QAOA design is worth its qubit and depth budget before running expensive optimization.
method: Define the finite-depth accessible set R_p(M,x0) for a chosen feasible start state, mixer schedule, and circuit depth.
Upper-bound achievable objective quality with f_R^* = max_{x in R_p} f(x) and normalize it as reachable-quality Q_R.
Test block-local XY mixer schedules on constrained portfolio optimization and synthetic block-constrained quadratic problems, including compilation-cost analysis.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 207 favorable-tail CVaR QAOA configurations, Q_R had the strongest association with realized shallow-QAOA performance among the structural diagnostics, with Pearson 0.7003 and Spearman 0.8057 correlations.
infographic.watch_item: The accessible-set diagnostic depends on the specific initial state, finite depth, and compiled mixer/phase-separator routing, so results may change substantially under different circuit synthesis choices or hardware constraints.
infographic.paper_title: Beyond Feasibility: Finite-Depth Accessibility in Constrained QAOA

title: Random Quantum Circuits Beyond Moment Matching
authors: Shih-Han Hung
abstract: Random quantum circuits aim to efficiently reproduce the statistical properties of ideal random quantum evolution. One approach is to construct approximate unitary designs, which match the moments of Haar-random unitaries up to a prescribed order with controlled error. In this work, we establish quantitative guarantees for how accurately these designs reproduce the full distributions of individual output probabilities. We show that, for every strong $\varepsilon$-approximate unitary $k$-design on $n$ qubits, the distribution of each individual output probability is within $O\left(\sqrt{\frac{2^n}{k(k+2^n)}}+\varepsilon\right)$ in Kolmogorov distance of the finite-dimensional Porter-Thomas distribution, a beta distribution with parameters $1$ and $2^n-1$. This bound is optimal up to constant factors, implying that a substantially better uniform bound requires additional structure. We further show that local invariance yields an exponential improvement in the dependence on $k$, with guarantees also in the stronger metric of total variation: every strong $\varepsilon$-approximate unitary $k$-design invariant under unitary translations acting on $\log k+O(1)$ qubits achieves error $2^{-Ω(k)}+O(\varepsilon)$ in Kolmogorov distance and $2^{-Ω(k)}+O(\varepsilon\log(2/\varepsilon))$ in total variation distance. These results identify both the distributional accuracy guaranteed by moment matching and the additional structure that substantially improves it. As an application, we show that if the marginal distribution of each output probability of a strong approximate design is within Kolmogorov distance $η$ of its Haar counterpart, then the expected Shannon entropy of the output distribution differs from its Haar value by $O(\sqrtη)$.

infographic.key_insight: Moment matching alone gives a quantified but limited approximation to Haar-random output probabilities; adding local invariance sharply improves the full distributional accuracy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For quantum circuit designers, this clarifies when approximate unitary designs are sufficient for randomness-sensitive metrics like output-probability statistics and entropy.
method: Proved Kolmogorov-distance bounds between single-output probabilities of strong approximate unitary k-designs and the finite-dimensional Porter-Thomas law.
Showed the bound scales as O(sqrt(2^n/(k(k+2^n))) + ε) and is optimal up to constants.
Identified extra local translation invariance on O(log k) qubits as a structure that improves errors to 2^{-Ω(k)} in Kolmogorov distance and total variation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports analytical guarantees and optimality results, not an empirical benchmark, with additional entropy-error bounds derived from the distributional distance result.
infographic.watch_item: The strongest improvements require extra local invariance beyond generic approximate k-designs, so standard design constructions may not achieve the exponential error decay.
infographic.paper_title: Random Quantum Circuits Beyond Moment Matching

title: Optimal transducers using symmetries
authors: Benoît Dubus, Julien Ladeuze, Jérémie Roland
abstract: Transducers (Belovs, Jeffery and Yolcu, 2024) are a quantum computing framework describing a quantum algorithm as a unitary converting an input state into a target state using a catalyst, an auxiliary vector that is left unchanged. They are a powerful tool in quantum algorithm design, especially in the context of quantum query complexity: feasible points of the (dual) adversary semidefinite program directly translate into transducers and the optimal transduction complexity is equal to the adversary bound, i.e. the Las Vegas complexity, which is known to characterize bounded-error quantum query complexity. Moreover, contrary to bounded-error algorithms, transducers compose exactly, which limits overheads due to controlling errors in algorithms constructed by composition. Constructing efficient, let alone optimal, transducers in terms of quantum query complexity nevertheless remains a hard task since it still requires solving the adversary SDP and constructing the unitary to obtain an explicit algorithm. In this paper, we show how using the symmetry group of state-conversion problems simplifies both steps. First, using a symmetrization argument, we prove an optimal catalyst can always be chosen covariant under a representation of the symmetry group. Second, we prove that the transducer intertwines two different representations of the group and can thus be chosen block diagonal in the isotypic decomposition of the Hilbert space. Using those methods, we then derive optimal transducers, with optimal constants, for different widely used quantum algorithmic primitives, such as unstructured search, amplitude amplification and amplitude estimation. Our approach extends previous work on the use of representation theory to compute adversary lower bounds (Høyer, Lee, and {\v S}palek, 2007; Ambainis, Magnin, Roetteler and Roland, 2011) to the systematic construction of optimal algorithms.

infographic.key_insight: By exploiting symmetry, the paper turns the hard problem of constructing optimal quantum transducers into a structured block-diagonal design problem, enabling exact optimal algorithms for several standard primitives.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives quantum algorithm designers a practical route to reduce query complexity overheads and build composition-friendly subroutines for search, amplitude amplification, and amplitude estimation.
method: Symmetrize the adversary-based optimization so the optimal catalyst respects the problem’s group symmetry.
Use representation theory to show the transducer intertwines group representations and decomposes block-diagonally.
Construct explicit optimal transducers within each isotypic block to recover optimal constants.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports optimal transducers with optimal constants for unstructured search, amplitude amplification, and amplitude estimation.
infographic.watch_item: The approach still depends on identifying the relevant symmetry group and performing representation-theoretic decomposition, which may be nontrivial for less structured problems.
infographic.paper_title: Optimal transducers using symmetries

title: QUFIG: GNN-Based Prediction of Quantum Fault Injection Vulnerabilities with Gate-Level Precision
authors: Shihan Zhao, Qiying Li, Ben Dong, Qian Wang, Yuntao Liu
abstract: The growing scale and accessibility of quantum hardware exposed new reliability and security challenges in the quantum computing workflow, such as the run-time fault injection attacks in cloud-based quantum computing platforms. However, existing works fail to identify vulnerabilities with gate-level precision or adapt to run-time environments. In this work, we formulate gate-level fault analysis as a learning-guided prioritization problem under restricted fidelity budgets. The framework uses a circuit-DAG-based GNN backbone to predict the vulnerability score of each gate to each type of injected fault, defined as the impact of the gate-fault pair on circuit fidelity. The gate-fault pairs are then ranked by their vulnerability score. Experiments on QASMbench and HamLib MaxCut show that QUFIG recovers high-impact vulnerable gate-fault pairs with fewer inspections than random and depth-based heuristics. Our results show that QUFIG can reduce the number of gates requiring inspection by 2.9--19.8% while maintaining effective fault identification, allowing quantum circuit designers to identify vulnerabilities and apply targeted defenses more efficiently.

infographic.key_insight: QUFIG uses a circuit-DAG GNN to rank gate-fault pairs by vulnerability, enabling gate-level quantum fault injection analysis with precision.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It helps quantum engineers prioritize which gates to inspect and harden first under limited verification budgets in cloud quantum workflows.
method: Builds a circuit-DAG graph representation of the quantum circuit.
Uses a GNN backbone to predict vulnerability scores for each gate-fault pair.
Ranks pairs by predicted impact on circuit fidelity for inspection prioritization.
infographic.evidence_signal: On QASMbench and HamLib MaxCut, QUFIG finds high-impact vulnerable pairs with fewer inspections than random and depth-based heuristics, reducing gates needing inspection by 2.9–19.8%.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on the quality of the circuit graph representation and the training/evaluation coverage of fault types, so generalization to unseen hardware or attack patterns may need validation.
infographic.paper_title: QUFIG: GNN-Based Prediction of Quantum Fault Injection Vulnerabilities with Gate-Level Precision

title: Efficient Calculation of Equilibrium Correlation Functions
authors: Yizhi Shen, Roel Van Beeumen, Wibe A. de Jong, Efekan Kökcü
abstract: A majority of measurable dynamic quantities of a physical system is described as an equilibrium correlation function of the form $G_{AB}(t-t') = \left<A(t)B(t')\right>$, where $t'$ represents the impact time and $t$ represents the response time. Conventional quantum algorithms to compute such quantities via Hamiltonian simulation such as the Hadamard test, variational methods, or linear-response-based algorithms share one feature in common: each time point $t-t'$ is calculated by a different quantum circuit, leading to at least $O(N_t)$ total shots, and at least $O(N_t^2)$ total quantum gates. Here, we provide a different approach: utilizing $O(\log N_t)$ ancilla qubits to store time as a quantum variable, and effectively parallelize the computation of an equilibrium correlation function by requiring only a single quantum circuit for all time points. We show that this circuit needs to be run only $O(\log N_t)$ times, which in total requires $O(N_t \log N_t)$ quantum resources in the large system size limits. We prove that this scaling is optimal, and demonstrate our algorithm calculating the Green's function of a one-dimensional spinless Hubbard model.

infographic.key_insight: The paper encodes time as a quantum variable with O(log N_t) ancilla qubits, allowing one circuit to evaluate equilibrium correlation functions for all time points in parallel.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This reduces repeated circuit construction and execution for dynamic observables, offering a more scalable path to Green's functions and other response calculations on quantum hardware.
method: Store time indices in O(log N_t) ancilla qubits.
Use a single quantum circuit to process all time points simultaneously.
Run the circuit only O(log N_t) times, yielding O(N_t log N_t) total resources in the large-system limit.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract states the method is proven optimal and demonstrated on the Green's function of a one-dimensional spinless Hubbard model.
infographic.watch_item: The approach still depends on fault-tolerant-looking resource scaling and may face practical overhead from ancilla control, circuit depth, and Hamiltonian simulation accuracy on near-term devices.
infographic.paper_title: Efficient Calculation of Equilibrium Correlation Functions
